title: Count Mentions Per User
statement:
A chat has `numberOfUsers` users with ids `0` to `numberOfUsers - 1`, and all of them start out online. Each entry of `events` is three strings `[type, timestamp, data]`, where `timestamp` is a whole number written as text. The events can be listed in any order of time.

- `["OFFLINE", timestamp, id]`: user `id` goes offline at `timestamp` and is back online automatically at `timestamp + 60`. That user is guaranteed to be online when this event happens.
- `["MESSAGE", timestamp, data]`: a message that mentions users. `data` is `"ALL"` (every user, online or not), `"HERE"` (every user who is online at that moment), or one or more tokens `id<number>` separated by single spaces, such as `"id1 id0 id1"`. Tokens name users directly, offline ones included, and a repeated token counts once per occurrence.

Whenever status changes (going offline or coming back online) and messages share a timestamp, the status changes are applied first. Return an array of length `numberOfUsers` whose entry `i` is the total number of times user `i` was mentioned.
constraints: A message listing ids has between 1 and 100 of them
Every id is between 0 and numberOfUsers - 1
The user of an OFFLINE event is online at that time
notes:
## Intuition

Whether a `HERE` message reaches a user depends on what happened before it in time, so the events must be replayed in time order, and the input does not promise that order. There is no need to keep online and offline sets or timers: remember for each user the moment `onlineAt[user]` from which they are online again. A user is online at time `t` exactly when `onlineAt[user] <= t`.

## Approach

1. Sort a copy of the events by numeric timestamp, putting OFFLINE before MESSAGE on equal timestamps, because status changes come first.
2. OFFLINE: set `onlineAt[user] = now + 60`.
3. `ALL`: add 1 for every user.
4. `HERE`: add 1 for every user with `onlineAt[user] <= now`.
5. Anything else is a list of tokens: split it on spaces and add 1 for each `id<number>`, repeats included.

## Example 1, step by step

The events are already in time order. At 10, `"id1 id0"` makes `mentions = [1, 1]`. At 11, user 0 goes offline, so `onlineAt = [71, 0]`. At 71, `HERE` checks `onlineAt[0] = 71 <= 71`: user 0 is back, so both users are mentioned and `mentions = [2, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m log m + m · (n + w)) for m events, n users and at most w tokens per message.
- Space: O(m + n) for the sorted copy, `mentions` and `onlineAt`.

## Pitfalls

- Timestamps are strings: compare them as numbers, or `"100"` sorts before `"20"`.
- On a shared timestamp the status change wins, both for going offline and for coming back at `timestamp + 60`.
- `ALL` reaches offline users too; `HERE` does not.
- A user named twice in one message is counted twice.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rank` | 0 for OFFLINE and 1 for MESSAGE, to break timestamp ties |
| `sorted` | the events in the order they are processed |
| `mentions` | mention count per user (the answer) |
| `onlineAt[user]` | first time the user is online again (0 at the start) |
| `type`, `time`, `data` | the current event's fields |
| `now` | the timestamp as a number |
| `token` | one `id<number>` of a message |

narration.2: rank breaks timestamp ties: OFFLINE (0) is handled before MESSAGE (1).
narration.3: Replay the events in time order, comparing timestamps as numbers rather than text.
narration.4: mentions[user] counts how often each user has been mentioned.
narration.5: onlineAt[user] is the first moment the user is online again; 0 means online from the start.
narration.7: Take the events one at a time, in sorted order.
narration.8: The timestamp arrives as text, so turn it into a number.
narration.10: ...keeps that user away until 60 time units later.
narration.11: ALL reaches every user, online or offline.
narration.13: Count one mention for this user.
narration.15: HERE reaches only the users who are online right now.
narration.17: A user is online once the current time has reached onlineAt.
narration.22: Otherwise the text is a list of id<number> tokens separated by spaces.
narration.23: Drop the id prefix and count the mention, repeats included.
narration.27: Return the counts for every user.
